To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the peptide 1–20 is a DR1-restrictive T cell epitope of the 19 kD protein of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
a mycobacterial peptide (residue 1-20) was identified as a T cell epitope that is recognized in the context of the DR1 MHC class II molecule by T cells of two patients with tuberculosis.
the mycobacterial peptide 1- 20 is a novel T cell epitope and that chemically unrelated peptides can compete in T cell recognition of mycobacterial epitopes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and characterization of a DR1-restriction mycobacterial peptide that stimulates T cell responses.
the identification of T cell epitopes in mycobacterial antigens, the characterization of their MHC restriction and the identification of competitors that can inhibit the antigen recognition.
the identification of mycobacterial peptides that stimulate cell-mediated responses in human patients with tuberculosis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
chemically unrelated mycobacteria-derived peptides can act as antigens and as competitors in antigen recognition of human T cells.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the DR1-restricted epitopes from two chemically different mycobacterial proteins are able to compete with each other in the recognition by human T cell.
chemically unrelated mycobacteria-derived peptides can compete in antigen recognition by DR1-restricted human mycobacterial T cells.

the mycobacterial competitor peptide 65-84 was able to inhibit the antigen recognition by a mycobacterial peptide, suggesting that the peptide 65-80 is able to bind to the DR1 molecule, thus preventing the binding of the peptide 1 to 20.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the 19-kDa protein of M. bovis contains a DR1-restrict T cell epitope.
the peptide 1–20 of the 19 kD protein is a T cell epitope of M. tuberculosis.
mycobacterial antigens and peptides can be used as antigens and as competitors in antigen recognition.
